analysis.one_liner: Lets workers take race discrimination claims to court instead of forced private arbitration.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate on November 20, 2025 with 10 Democratic sponsors, referred to the Judiciary Committee, where no further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: Most employment contracts make workers sign away their right to sue before a dispute ever exists, forcing race discrimination and harassment claims into private arbitration where proceedings are confidential and there is no jury or class action. This bill would let anyone alleging race, color, or national origin discrimination choose to go to court instead, and would invalidate agreements that also bar them from joining class or collective actions. A judge, not an arbitrator, would decide whether the law applies. The change would apply to claims that arise after the bill became law.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and job applicants who allege race, color, or national origin discrimination or retaliation. They could elect to have their case heard in a public court, with a jury and the possibility of joining a class or collective action, even if they previously signed an arbitration agreement. Women and members of other protected groups could also benefit, since race and sex discrimination claims often overlap.

how_it_helps.text: At the election of the person alleging discrimination, no predispute arbitration agreement or predispute joint-action waiver would be valid or enforceable for a court case relating to race, color, or national origin discrimination under federal, Tribal, state, or local law [S2].
The bill covers discrimination, harassment, and retaliation, matching the legal grounds workers commonly allege in workplace cases [S2].

Whether the law applies would be decided by a judge rather than an arbitrator, and the election could also be made by a class or collective-action representative, keeping group cases out of arbitration [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers lose a routine tool: the pre-dispute arbitration clause that keeps discrimination cases out of court and out of the public record. Cases would be more expensive to defend in litigation, and public court rulings could create reputational and legal precedent costs. Arbitration providers lose potential caseload.

drawbacks.text: The bill covers only race, color, and national origin claims, leaving other forms of workplace discrimination such as sex, age, or disability still subject to forced arbitration unless Congress extends the same rule to them [S2].

Litigation in court costs employers more and moves more slowly than arbitration, and employers argue arbitration can be faster and cheaper for workers too; the bill does not attempt to regulate arbitration quality, it simply takes race discrimination claims out of the system entirely [S2].
Only Democrats have signed on, and the bill has seen no committee action since referral, so its narrow scope and partisan start make passage in this Congress unlikely [S1][S3][S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to workers is real: public court cases produce binding precedent, juries, and a public record, while confidential arbitration can make repeat discrimination invisible. The costs fall on employers in the form of litigation expense and exposure, and the law is deliberately narrower than the underlying problem — it addresses race discrimination but leaves forced arbitration in place for most other disputes. On balance, it removes a barrier that systematically advantages the party that drafted the contract.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which has not taken it up.

narrative.text: Senator Booker introduced the bill on November 20, 2025, joined by nine Democratic senators [S1][S2].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary, the same day [S4].
No further action appears in the record since that referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one yet; the bill is awaiting committee action, and employers' forced arbitration practices remain unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody yet; bill awaits committee action

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee

against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on November 20, 2025; no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled, leaving it without a path to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All ten original sponsors are Democrats, and no Republican has joined; there has been no roll-call vote.

industries.note: Pre-dispute arbitration clauses let employers move race discrimination claims into confidential arbitration without juries or class actions. The bill would let workers opt out of those clauses for race, color, and national origin claims, raising employer litigation costs and creating public records of discrimination cases [S2].
Private arbitration firms such as the American Arbitration Association and JAMS would lose potential caseload from workplace race discrimination disputes [S2].

industries.industry: Plaintiffs' employment and civil rights bar
industries.note: Civil rights attorneys would gain court work from race discrimination cases that arbitration clauses previously removed, including class and collective actions [S2].

analysis.trajectory: Bills that sit in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a hearing or markup this late in the first session rarely reach the floor. With no Republican cosponsors, the bill likely stalls unless its sponsor builds bipartisan support; a comparable 2022 law ending forced arbitration for sexual assault and harassment claims passed only after bipartisan sponsorship, which this bill does not yet have.
